title: Mystery, complexity, legibility and coherence: A meta-analysis
review_question: To calculate how well the four informational variables (mystery, complexity, legibility, coherence) predict preferences for environments.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Studies were included if they provided sufficient data to calculate a correlation between preference and at least one of the four informational variables, had sufficient data for 'n', included at least four correlations for weight calculation, used a unique set of environments, and adhered to the operational definitions of the four variables. Studies using colored slides/photographs were preferred, but black and white/graphic representations were included as 'dubious'. Studies using small expert panels for informational variable ratings were classified as 'dubious'. Excluded were narrative reviews, duplicate publications, duplicate use of stimuli, discursive or ordinal effect sizes, and different variable definitions.

synthesis_conclusions: The Kaplan informational model (mystery, complexity, legibility, coherence predicting preference) has not generated reproducible results.
The 'Category Identification Method' (CIM) for describing environments did not generate reproducible categories.

Studies using 'expert panels' to rate informational variables produced significantly different (smaller) correlations with preference for coherence, legibility, and complexity compared to studies where the same population rated both preference and informational variables.
Dividing stimuli into 'natural' and 'built' categories did not resolve the heterogeneity problem for complexity and mystery correlations with preference.
Correlations of preference with coherence and legibility differed significantly between natural and built scenes (higher for built scenes).
The range of correlations for all four informational variables with preference is very wide, making the degree and direction of relationships currently unknown.
evidence_gaps: Need for more reproducible methods for measuring informational concepts (e.g., objective measures like visibility polygons for mystery, entropy for complexity, or behavioral measures like looking time).
Need for larger studies, especially for legibility and for detecting differences between natural and built scenes for complexity and mystery.
Further investigation into the effect of 'dissertation versus published work' on study quality.
Replication with urban scenes for legibility and coherence.
risk_of_bias_assessment: Identified concerns include selective reporting of results (publication bias), use of small 'expert panels' for ratings, use of black and white photographs, and reporting partial correlations or correlations based on multidimensional plots rather than raw data. Dubious studies were analyzed separately to assess their impact.
heterogeneity_sources: Differences in experimental protocols (e.g., use of expert panels vs. same population for ratings).
Use of black and white photographs vs. color.
Reporting partial correlations vs. raw data.
The irreproducibility of the 'Category Identification Method' (CIM) categories.
The wide range of correlation values across studies for all four informational variables.
The possibility that the problems lie with the original material/theory, not the meta-analysis method.
publication_bias: Selective reporting of results (only 'p<0.05' correlations) was identified as a concern. Correlations calculated but not published were assigned an expected value of zero to mitigate this bias.

moderators.effect: Solid studies produced significantly higher correlations for coherence (r=0.46 vs. r=0.23), legibility (r=0.22 vs. r=-0.01), and complexity (r=0.32 vs. r=0.15) with preference compared to dubious studies. No significant difference was found for mystery (r=0.42 vs. r=0.44).
moderators.subgroup_effects: Coherence: solid r=0.46, dubious r=0.23. Legibility: solid r=0.22, dubious r=-0.01. Complexity: solid r=0.32, dubious r=0.15. Mystery: solid r=0.42, dubious r=0.44.

moderators.effect: Correlations of preference with coherence and legibility were significantly different between natural and built scenes (higher for built scenes). No significant difference was found for complexity or mystery.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Coherence: natural r=0.31, built r=0.72. Legibility: natural r=-0.25, built r=0.52. Complexity: natural r=0.26, built r=0.42. Mystery: natural r=0.49, built r=0.26.

limitations: Small number of experiments in some sub-classifications.
The 'Category Identification Method' (CIM) for describing environments has not generated reproducible results.
The use of 'expert panels' (3-8 people) for rating informational variables is a weak link in the research.
Lack of power for some contrasts (e.g., for complexity and mystery differences between natural and built scenes).
The pervasive heterogeneity across findings makes collective correlations misleading.

theory_commitments.theory_name: Kaplan & Kaplan's Information Processing Theory of Environmental Preference
theory_commitments.specific_claim: Environmental preferences are influenced by four informational dimensions: coherence, complexity, legibility, and mystery, which facilitate understanding and exploration.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper synthesizes evidence for how perceived environmental qualities (coherence, mystery, complexity, legibility) influence human preference through their impact on information processing and understanding.
